tools.title: The White House needs a ground stop
tools.summary_raw: On Still Counting EP13, we discussed a chaotic Friday the 13th and a White House that hasn’t learned anything from the midterms.
tools.content_text: Sean Duffy and Markwayne Mullin brief the press on Nov. 13 amid an FAA ground stop. Alex Wong/Getty Images. Buckle your seatbelts, because Galen, Clare, and I got a little more wound up than usual on this week’s Still Counting, where we discussed the Nvidia story/scandal and the nationwide ground stop on Friday, just the second since Sept. 11. It’s hard not to feel that way when the Secretary of Transportation has trouble explaining WTF was going on. It’s been a highly turbulent two weeks for the White House since the midterms, and with 793 more days remaining in President Trump’s term, we’re nowhere near our final descent into God-knows-what. Pressing for an analogy, I likened the current course to the prolonged and gory denouement of the movie The Substance . 1 Video above, audio below. Like always, we appreciate any comments, likes , reviews and subscribes. The context Unless there’s another disruption around the holidays, the ground stop that the FAA ordered late Friday afternoon probably won’t be remembered as a seminal political event. And I don’t think it should be, although maybe I’d feel differently if I were stranded on the tarmac at LaGuardia at the time. However, I think it represents an unusually clean natural experiment. Something serious but not that serious happened. It was unplanned, and the government needed to respond. It’s not something like the Nvidia story, which has incredibly wide-ranging implications and would be a communications challenge for any White House to deal with regardless of the president. Instead, the communication surrounding the ground stop ought to have been fairly basic political blocking-and-tackling, a test of whether you’re executing your fundamentals. It’s also one of the first such tests after Democrats swept into power two weeks ago in an historic repudiation of President Trump . Is the White House making any adjustments to acknowledge that Americans are sick of how they’ve handled business? No. I don’t have anything in particular against Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, although he doesn’t have any obvious qualifications for the job, having been : a nationally-recognized lumberjack, a Real World contestant, a sportscaster, a prosecutor and district attorney, a 5-term U.S. Representative from Wisconsin, a senior counsel for a lobbying firm, and a CNN and Fox News contributor. It’s kind of a fun resumé, but there’s not much obviously transit-related. (To be fair, the previous secretary of transportation, Pete Buttigieg, didn’t have many transportation-adjacent credentials either.) Subscribe now But Trump presumably chose Duffy because he watches a lot of TV, and Duffy has been on TV a lot. He’s at least supposed to look and act the part. I don’t want to turn Silver Bulletin into a #Resistance blog that chronicles every minor outrage of the Trump administration. But for some reason, I felt triggered by the press conference that Duffy and the Homeland Security Secretary, former Oklahoma Sen. […]

market.title: How The Times and Sunday Times build communities through comments
market.summary_raw: "Community is a very difficult thing to put a metric on," says Rachel Duffy of The Times and Sunday Times. However, communities are also crucial areas for all news publishers, and something that has been mentioned by several speakers during our Newsroom Summit conference in Oslo. For The Times, a natural area to focus on is their comments section.
market.content_text: The Times has been around since 1785, and today has nearly 700,000 paid digital subscribers. Like many news publishers, retaining paying subscribers is vital for The Times, Rachel Duffy , Head of Community for The Times & The Sunday Times, told participants at our Newsroom Summit conference. “How do we make sure that they stay?” Duffy asked. “We needed to make them feel like they are part of a community.” One key way The Times and Sunday Times is doing this is by taking an area already popular with their readers – the comments section – and then doubling down to make the most of it. The Times gets about 650,000 comments a month, Duffy said, and 41 percent of their readers regularly read the comments section. The Times aims to drive comments for all news and opinions articles, “and to do so in ways that encourage better comments as a result,” she said. While they are interested in getting more comments, they don’t want growth to come at the expense of quality, Duffy said. “We’ve spent a lot of time designing platforms that measure the quality of our comments, so it’s not just about increasing that volume,” she said. “Seventy percent of all Times readers live in our app,” Duffy noted, adding that they’ve put a considerable amount of time and investment into making sure the app is the place to be. WAN-IFRA’s Newsroom Summit brought together 125+ delegates from 30 countries on five continents. We’re gathered at Verdens Gang (VG) , Norway’s leading digital media house, in Oslo for this two-day event. Photo by Tom Atle Bordevik / Bordevik.no . ‘Meet readers where they already are’ As is the case for many other publishers, a relatively small percentage of consumers actually write comments, but many users are interested in reading them. In fact, the percentage of Times users who read the comments section is between a third and a half, Duffy noted. And as mentioned earlier, just over 40 percent of the time those users spend with a piece of content is now spent reading its related comments, she said. “We’re just trying to meet readers where they already are,” she said. Duffy has a team of four. “We moderate the comments, we place conversation starters and polls.” “We want it to be a positive place. We don’t want our readers’ first experience of the comments section to be a negative experience, so we’re spending a lot of time moderating in the traditional sense of the word, but we’re also bringing in new voices,” she said. Getting their journalists involved How that works in practice is that The Times encourages its writers to go into the comments section to do more of their journalism, Duffy said. “It wasn’t about building another product to engage readers or spend a lot of time on marketing to encourage them to go to a new section of the app. They’re already there in the comments section.” “On a data point, this is brilliant for our dwell time. If you remove the comments section, you can see the impact that would have on dwell time. […]

market.title: WAN-IFRA stands with AMI in condemning the attack on Panamanian journalist Rolando Rodríguez
market.summary_raw: WAN-IFRA, the World Association of News Publishers, joins its member association AMI, the Asociación de Medios de Información, and the Inter American Press Association (IAPA) in condemning the attack on the home of Rolando Rodríguez, associate deputy editor of the Panamanian daily La Prensa.
market.content_text: Rodríguez is known for his investigations into corruption, public procurement and the use of public funds, and for his work on the Panama Papers. When the attack happened, he was preparing a new investigation and he was also part of an international team looking into alleged multimillion-dollar deals involving the marketing of Venezuelan crude oil. Last March, at the IX CELAC-EU Editors’ Congress in Alcalá de Henares, he received the EditoRed award in recognition of his dedicated and outstanding work in investigative journalism . At the same ceremony, AMI’s Director General, Irene Lanzaco, received the EditoRed award for her career in defence of journalism . At about 2:30 a.m. on Saturday, 14 November, an individual arrived at Rodríguez’s home by taxi and threw an explosive device, which caused an explosion and a fire. The fire destroyed the two vehicles parked in the garage and damaged the roof. His wife was inside and escaped unharmed. Rodríguez was out of the city at the time. The National Police and the Public Prosecutor’s Office have opened investigations, and police arrested a first suspect on Sunday, 15 November. AMI stressed that no journalist should have to fear for their own safety or that of their family because of their work. The IAPA called the attack “a brutal act of intimidation that must not go unpunished.” WAN-IFRA joins AMI and the IAPA in calling on the Panamanian authorities to: carry out a prompt, thorough and independent investigation that identifies both those who carried out the attack and those who ordered it, so that it does not go unpunished; determine whether the attack was retaliation for La Prensa’s reporting; guarantee the protection of Rodríguez, his family and La Prensa’s journalists, so that they can keep working without threats or retaliation.

market.title: WAN-IFRA renews call for Yuki Imai’s release at Oslo summit
market.summary_raw: Japanese journalist Yuki Imai’s imprisonment in Russia brought the defence of press freedom into focus at WAN-IFRA’s Newsroom Summit, where Norwegian Parliament President Masud Gharahkhani urged the media to keep challenging power.
market.content_text: The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) renewed its call for the immediate release of Japanese journalist Yuki Imai at the opening of the Newsroom Summit , taking place in Oslo on November 18-19. Addressing more than 100 newsroom leaders from 30 countries, WAN-IFRA CEO Stig Ørskov highlighted a colleague denied the freedom to report. Imai, a correspondent for Japan’s Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested on Sakhalin Island on October 13 and remains in Moscow’s Lefortovo prison, where Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich was also held. Russia accuses Imai of espionage, an allegation rejected by Japan. He was working with a journalist visa and Russian foreign ministry accreditation. “His case reminds us that the freedom to ask questions can never be taken for granted,” Ørskov said. Imai covered Russia’s Far East and its regional relationships. His final dispatch before his arrest described the everyday lives of North Korean workers on Sakhalin. His continued detention has prompted warnings from press freedom organisations against using journalists as political bargaining instruments. WAN-IFRA called for his immediate release on November 4. The Japan Newspaper Publishers & Editors Association, NSK, has also demanded his release and urged intensified diplomatic efforts to bring him home. “A free press is supposed to challenge those in power” Speaking at the Summit, President of the Norwegian Parliament, Masud Gharahkhani, delivered a clear defence of independent journalism and its role in democracy. “A free press is not supposed to make those in power comfortable. A free press is supposed to challenge those in power,” he said. “That is not a weakness of democracy. It is one of its greatest strengths.” He warned that press freedom faces threats within democracies as well as in authoritarian states, pointing to harassment, polarisation, declining trust and disinformation. “That means we cannot take press freedom for granted. Not anywhere. Not even in our own societies.” Norway’s strong tradition of press freedom carries a responsibility to support those denied it elsewhere, he said. “And together, we must support those around the world who are still fighting for the freedoms we often take for granted.”

market.title: How GMA’s DigiLab turns social memes into real reporting
market.summary_raw: In an increasingly inter-connected world, a younger audience brings different challenges for newsrooms, which face mounting pressure to overhaul traditional formats while retaining viewership.
market.content_text: By Bing Hong “The question for us in the newsrooms is no longer just about what stories we tell them, but also how and where to tell them,” says Gabrielle Cayetano, Senior Media Strategist of Philippines-based GMA News. Speaking at WAN-IFRA’s recent Asian Media Leaders Summit in Singapore, Cayetano discussed how adapting to and appealing to a younger audience might well hold the key to newsroom sustainability. Reflecting on her household’s transition from watching late-night, free-to-air television newscasts with her father to following news online via YouTube, Cayetano’s own experiences as a Gen Z reinforces her belief that shifting habits demand a fresh editorial approach. ‘My FYP is not an audience research report’ Cayetano cautioned against over-relying on personal anecdotes or stereotypes when designing content strategy, especially for younger audiences. “My own news consumption habits don’t represent an entire generation,” Cayetano said, noting that while she personally dislikes podcasts, many of her peers consume them daily. “What simply works for me might not work for you, and what might work for you doesn’t mean that it will work for me.” She added that GMA News Digital Lab operates under a clear rule: “My For You page is not an audience research report.” To that end, her team focuses on three aspects: D eveloping digital-native coverage T esting non-traditional storytelling formats, and Using audience data to inform editorial coverage The balancing act: Combining viral hooks with serious context But therein lies the rub: how exactly do organisations know if they are actually reaching their audiences? “That’s where understanding our audiences comes in, because sometimes audiences respond to our stories or to our content differently from how we expect them to,” Cayetano said. For DigiLab, testing how certain media formats performed revealed critical insights about audience retention. When refining their flagship digital program, GMA News Feed, DigiLab shifted from viral user-generated clips (which drew 127.4 million views in Q1) to purely serious news explainers in Q2. Views promptly dropped to 51.8 million. Rather than abandoning the latter, the team introduced a balanced hybrid model in Q3, pairing viral human-interest hooks with the explainers. Views surged to 364.5 million, surpassing the earlier two quarters. “These types of content complement each other in tapping diverse audiences,” Cayetano added. […]

market.title: WAN-IFRA Partners with News Product Alliance to Drive Innovation at the 2027 San Francisco AI Forum
market.summary_raw: WAN-IFRA has partnered with the News Product Alliance on its San Francisco AI Forum, bringing international AI leaders and senior US product executives together at KQED on 25–26 January 2027.
market.content_text: The World Association of News Publishers has announced a strategic partnership with the News Product Alliance for the San Francisco AI Forum . Hosted at KQED in the world’s technology capital, the event takes place January 25-26, 2027. The Forum brings senior U.S. product, audience, AI, and engineering leaders together with AI executives and experts from WAN-IFRA’s international network of publishers in San Francisco. “ AI is changing how publishers develop products, serve audiences and organise their businesses. Our San Francisco AI Forum, developed in partnership with the News Product Alliance, brings together visionaries and practitioners to share what they are learning and help publishers make better decisions. By combining WAN-IFRA’s global network with NPA’s product-first mindset, we want to help publishers build news products that audiences trust, value and are willing to pay for ,” said Stig Ørskov, CEO of WAN-IFRA. The two-day event is designed to address the most urgent questions facing product and newsroom leaders today, including how to earn revenue in a market with no settled model, how to scale AI adoption across a newsroom, and how to prioritise effectively in an era of rapid prototyping. “ AI has made it much faster to build things, but a newsroom still needs people who can decide what’s worth building and keep it running once it ships. That product capacity is what turns speed into something useful for audiences, and it’s what many product teams are working on right now. This Forum gives them a chance to compare notes with colleagues from around the world ,” said Becca Aaronson, NPA’s Chief Product Officer. Working closely with the WAN-IFRA team, NPA has helped shape a comprehensive programme featuring AI pioneers from the United States, the UK, Denmark, Sweden, and Taiwan. Key themes for the 2027 event include: Business Models and Monetisation: Assessing the rapidly changing market, clarifying demand, and navigating unsettled commercial models with a keynote by Mary Liz McCurdy, the senior vice president of business development and strategic partnerships at The Atlantic. Scaling AI Adoption: Strategies for newsrooms and news groups to support journalists in acquiring new skills and developing an AI-forward mindset from strategy to execution, with a session about Hearst Newspaper’s DevHub delivered by Tim O’Rourke, Vice President Editorial Innovation + AI Strategy, and Derrick Ho, AI & Editorial Strategy. Placing Bets and Prioritisation: Determining where to allocate time, capital, and executive attention in an accelerated prototyping environment. The NPA will lead discussions on how product management handles this new pace of development with a keynote by NPA board member Anita Zielina. […]

market.title: Election season lifted public radio sites. So did a Supreme Court scandal and license plate drama.
market.summary_raw: More than a year ago, NHPR reporter Todd Bookman started asking questions about “an irregular personnel maneuver” involving the chief justice of New Hampshire’s Supreme Court. Bookman’s reporting ultimately became “Exhibit A” in the ethics probe that led to the justice’s resignation in September. The bombshell resignation news was NHPR’s biggest story in September —...
market.content_text: More than a year ago, NHPR reporter Todd Bookman started asking questions about “an irregular personnel maneuver” involving the chief justice of New Hampshire’s Supreme Court. Bookman’s reporting ultimately became “Exhibit A” in the ethics probe that led to the justice’s resignation in September. The bombshell resignation news was NHPR’s biggest story in September — and of 2026 to date. The story helped push NHPR up several spots in our regular ranking of public radio websites. NHPR saw visits rise 22% that month, according to Similarweb visit figures compiled by Nieman Lab. At the very top of the list, not much moved. The Chicago Sun-Times , owned by Chicago Public Media, held onto the top spot, followed by Gothamist (from WNYC) and Minnesota Public Radio . As Nieman Lab senior writer Joshua Benton wrote when introducing the rankings , which we’ve also done for local newspapers and local nonprofit news sites , not all markets are created equal. Public radio stations serving major metropolitan areas with lots of college graduates have a bigger potential audience than stations serving smaller communities and areas with fewer resources. And, of course, Similarweb provides an estimate; internal metrics may differ. Still, the rankings are a valuable window into some industry-wide trends, and often an opportunity to highlight local news organizations punching above their weight. Like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. New Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, said NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott . She described September as a solid month, not an outlier. “But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said. “[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added. On the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.” BREAKING: Fearless reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp — Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026 WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. market.title: Federal funding for public media is coming back, one way or another. But is it time for a deeper rethink?
market.summary_raw: It was 318 days ago that the Corporation for Public Broadcasting — the primary funder of public media in the United States since 1967 — officially ceased to be, the victim of Republican budget cuts and years of attacks from Donald Trump. CPB is not “on pause” or “in hibernation” — it’s dead. As its...
market.content_text: It was 318 days ago that the Corporation for Public Broadcasting — the primary funder of public media in the United States since 1967 — officially ceased to be , the victim of Republican budget cuts and years of attacks from Donald Trump. CPB is not “on pause” or “in hibernation” — it’s dead. As its final CEO Patricia Harrison put it: “CPB’s final act would be to protect the integrity of the public media system and democratic values by dissolving, rather than allowing the organization to remain defunded and vulnerable to additional attacks.” You may have heard, however, that we had some elections in the U.S. recently, and the Republicans who defunded NPR and PBS will no longer control the House of Representatives or Senate as of January 3. In their place will be Congressional Democrats much more favorable to public media. So it seems quite likely that the federal government’s next budget will re-fund it rather than de-fund it. But with CPB officially no more, Democrats will have a rare opportunity to rethink the system from scratch instead of just prescribing minor tweaks to funding levels. The media environment of 2027 will, it goes without saying, be radically different from 1967’s. Over-the-air broadcasting is no longer America’s dominant medium. The immensely profitable newspapers that were the bedrock of news back then are shells of their former selves. And what was once a highly localized information ecosystem has been thoroughly nationalized and globalized, with access to news increasingly determined by a few large tech platforms. Democrats could just revive the old LBJ-era model — but should they instead build something new? These questions will dominate the next year of discourse around public media, and interested parties are already laying out plans. This morning, the Roosevelt Institute released a new white paper titled “Creating a New U.S. Public Media System: Normative Arguments and Policy Options.” Written by Penn professor (and past Nieman Lab contributor ) Victor Pickard , it argues for a thorough reinvention: But the fact that $30 billion sounds enormous is mostly about how small U.S. public media has always been compared to its international peers. Before defunding, the U.S. spent roughly $3 per person per year on public media. Compare that to countries like Norway ($110), Finland ($101), Denmark ($93), the U.K. ($81), France ($76), Czechia ($60), Japan ($53), Australia ($36), and Canada ($27). If Pickard got his $30 billion wish, U.S. public media funding would sit at about $88 per capita — BBC territory, roughly speaking. But even getting to the level of Canada or Australia would mean a huge increase. […]

market.title: After gutting newsrooms, McClatchy plans to rebuild itself around AI
market.summary_raw: Two months after McClatchy Media laid off more than 90 journalists nationwide, executives at the storied local newspaper chain offered a blunt assessment of its future. The award-winning local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old company was no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month,...
market.content_text: Two months after McClatchy Media laid off more than 90 journalists nationwide, executives at the storied local newspaper chain offered a blunt assessment of its future. The award-winning local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old company was no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month, and its survival depended on a wholesale reinvention — centered entirely around artificial intelligence. From the rollout of new lifestyle websites that feature AI-generated articles and sponsored content to legal review and finance, executives revealed how AI is now integrated into virtually every part of the company. The demonstration comes after McClatchy, one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates, carried out deep staff cuts in September at the Miami Herald, The Kansas City Star, and more than a dozen other local news outlets. An anonymous “person close to the executive decision-making” told The New York Times the layoffs were not about AI and were instead about “business performance in some areas.” “We cannot continue to do the same things because the marketplace has changed,” McClatchy CEO Tony Hunter told staff during the off-the-record Nov. 6 meeting, according to audio provided to Nieman Lab. Executives told staff that McClatchy-owned publications have suffered a 17% decline in paid digital subscribers in the last year — and unique visitors have plummeted 39%. [img wide] Photo of a slide with audience figures shown during the town hall meeting[/img] A companywide blueprint presented during the meeting highlights how McClatchy is systematically outsourcing the infrastructure for local news to AI agents — and rebranding around lifestyle verticals for sports fans, outdoor enthusiasts, and true-crime junkies. Dubbed “Project Catalyst,” the companywide restructure will create an “AI-native operating model” that takes “repeated tasks off of humans” and embeds AI agents “directly into the daily workflow,” Jeff Dorsey , McClatchy’s chief operating officer, said at the town hall. Dorsey described the initiative as an effort to automate “non-core as well as core functions,” “get rid of things that just don’t offer the same value” they once did, and “provide cash, frankly, to keep the business afloat.” McClatchy, which operates 29 daily newspapers across 14 states, didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment.
